problem: Existing 3D navigation simulators either lack human dynamics or, like iGibson-SN and Isaac Sim, offer few scenes and few human models and are computationally heavy. Prior crowd-aware navigation is mostly trained in 2D simulators with known human dynamics, which does not match egocentric visual perception.
motivation: Robots deployed to assist people must navigate crowded, dynamic spaces using only onboard sensors. A fast, photorealistic, diverse, large-scale 3D benchmark with well-designed human dynamics is missing, and so are crowdedness measures and collision-aware metrics.
key_idea: Add a continuous force-and-torque crowd model (UPL++, an extension of the universal power law) with 40 virtual humans to 480 HM3D scenes in Habitat 2.0, giving a fast crowd-aware visual navigation benchmark.
insight: Explicit or implicit recognition of humans from RGB-D is the key bottleneck: the ViT-based OVRL-v2 beats the other baselines in every density bin, while baselines that need human dynamics information (DS-RNN, LB-WPN) do worse. The collision-penalty ablation shows a trade-off: a larger penalty magnitude (-1e-4 to -1e-2) lowers collisions per distance but also SR and SPL. Adding the collision penalty (R^c = -1e-4) improves all methods over R^c = 0.
method: UPL++ human dynamics: a force model (adjusting force toward the goal, social force from the gradient of a time-to-collision interaction energy, PyBullet contact forces, random fluctuation) plus a new torque model that aligns orientation with velocity; O(n) complexity.

Dataset construction: MakeHuman avatars are placed in 480 HM3D scenes (400/40/40 train/val/test), 40 human models, densities 0.1-0.5 humans/m^2 (mean 0.226), navigation areas 10-300 m^2. Humans return to their start after reaching the goal so motion is continuous.
Built on Habitat 2.0: parallel, fast rendering with low memory (<400 MB RAM per scene).

Tasks and reward: point-goal and object-goal navigation with RGB-D only and no human dynamics given. Reward r_t = R^c*I_collision + R^s*I_success + R^f*(d_{t-1} - d_t) with R^s=2.5, R^f=1.0, and R^c=-1e-4 by default.
New metric CPD (collisions per distance traveled), used together with SR, SPL and DTG.
Benchmarks: five baselines (LB-WPN, DOA, DD-PPO, DS-RNN, OVRL-v2), each trained for 30M frames, plus analyses of human density and collision penalty.

setting.backbone: Baseline agents trained end-to-end: LB-WPN, DOA, DD-PPO, DS-RNN, OVRL-v2 (ViT)
setting.training_data: HabiCrowd, 400 train scenes, 30M frames per method
setting.privileged: none (human dynamics are not given to the agent)

numbers_note: Split names for the HabiCrowd benchmarks are not stated explicitly; 'test' is assumed. Simulator benchmarks (FPS, RAM, dynamics CAR 100%, GR 93.3%, mCT 0.012) are given in the paper but are not navigation results. The FPS/RAM figure values are only in figures.
results: HabiCrowd's UPL++ is collision-free (CAR 100%) with a goal-reaching rate of 93.3% (iGibson-SN: 94.1%), and it is about twice as fast (mCT 0.012 vs 0.023). The simulator renders about 3x faster than iGibson-SN and 2x faster than Isaac Sim. Among the navigation baselines, OVRL-v2 is best: point-goal SR 94.61 and object-goal SR 20.79, beating DOA (16.57) by 4.22 points on ObjectNav.
limitations: Humans move rigidly because of Habitat 2.0 constraints, which is far from real human motion.
No sim2real or real-robot evaluation; the baselines lack an explicit way to infer human dynamics from RGB-D.
The object-goal task remains very hard (SR at most about 21%).
